newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Lasertec sees higher profits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Lasertec sees higher profits.

text.p: Japanese electronic components firm Lasertec Corp is aiming for a parent current profit of around 1.3 billion yen next business year, up about 20 percent from its estimate for its financial year to June 30.

"Despite planned spending for building new offices and higher labour costs, we can still target a current profit of around 1.2 to 1.3 billion yen in the next business year, or up 20 percent from the estimated profit for the current year," Lasertec president Daikichi Awamura said in an interview.
"Profit per share may increase to 100 yen next year. If so, we would like to consider higher dividend payments," he said.
Lasertec, which was established in 1962, now enjoys a 70 percent global share of the market for photomask defect detectors which are used in semiconductor manufacturing.
By midday on Monday, the company's shares were trading at 3,620 yen on the over-the-counter market, unchanged from the Friday level. The firm went public in December 1990.

Higher orders for its mainstay product would help push the firm's sales to at least six billion yen next business year starting in April, up more than 20 percent from estimated sales for 1996/97, Awamura said.
For 1996/97, the company forecast parent sales of 4.85 billion yen and current profits of 1.02 billion yen, he said.

Awamura said the company expects orders for its mainstay products to have increased in January and February. Demand for photomask defect detectors is intensifying with semiconductor makers switching their focus to next-generation 64-megabit or 256-megabit semiconductor chips, he said.
"Since we enjoy a high market share, we face limited competition. Therefore, the prices for our products have not declined, which is to our advantage," he said.

Awamura said he was not worried about the possibility of new entrants in the photomask defect defector market, but added that the market was not large enough for big manufacturers to take part in. It would also take considerable time as well as costs to develop such high-tech products, he said.
The company plans to spend 110 million yen for research and development next business year, up from 97 million yen this year, he said.
Lasertec aims to expand sales to 10 billion yen in 2001, probably by moving into the new business area of making plasma display panel (PDP) defect detectors, he said.
